newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-GREENPEACE PLANS PROTEST OF GENETIC SOY SHIPMENT.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-GREENPEACE PLANS PROTEST OF GENETIC SOY SHIPMENT.

text.p: Environmentalists plan a protest when a ship docks in Hamburg late Tuesday with what they think are the first genetically-altered U.S. soybeans to reach Europe.
Greenpeace campaigners would not say what form the action would take against the freighter, Ideal Progress.
"These soybeans will be used as a precedent for other genetically altered crops, which are not desirable for food and farming," said Joerg Naumann, leader of the campaign.
"We want to put pressure on food processors to say no to these beans and we want farmers...to stop planting genetically altered seeds."
Health anxieties about biotechnology are most acute in Germany, where Greenpeace has gathered a list of 120,000 signatories to a consumer petition against modified soybeans.
Developed by chemicals giant Monsanto Co of the United States, the soybeans have been altered to resist a widely-used weedkiller.
Ideal Progress will have 44,600 tonnes of new crop soybeans aboard, shipped for Oelmuehle Hamburg (Oelag), a leading European processor.
"Production schedules have not been altered," said Arnd von Wissel, board head at the firm.
"There are customers waiting for the products."
As some one to two percent of the U.S. soybean crop is now made up of genetically-altered beans, Greenpeace says it is likely that some of this material is aboard Ideal Progress.
The campaigners want the food industry to boycott these beans or at least label products to tell consumers that they might have been derived from genetically-altered organisms.
"There are just too many unknown factors...what does it mean if you eat these products all your life and what does their existence do to the ecosystem?" asked Naumann.
Soya is used in some form or another in some 30,000 foodstuffs including margarine, chocolate and mayonnaise.

Some leading food firms, including the German unit of Anglo-Dutch Unilever, have already responded to German consumer concerns and said they will not sell products containing oils from modified beans, although they consider the beans safe.

The European Union said on Tuesday its Farm Commissioner, Franz Fischler, would discuss genetically altered grains among other issues when he meets U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman at a world food summit in Rome later this month. The protests may have cost the U.S. lost soybean exports, but Washington officals say supply and demand patterns have so far favoured export destinations other than Europe.
Crushers have said they could get around the German protest by exporting soy oil to other countries and supplying the domestic market with rapeseed and sunseed oil.
"I wouldn't call that responsible," said Naumann.
With the U.S. new crop in full swing, soybean ships are expected in Hamburg at 10-day intervals over the next few months. Another vessel is due in Ghent on Saturday.
The United States last year sold an estimated two million tonnes to Germany worth $690 million, accounting for two-thirds of Germany's soybean imports.
